transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Ever since I got shocked on that job, I feel this constant sense of dread and uneasiness that just won’t go away, even when I’m not at work. It's just... always there in the background, and I can't seem to shake it.
Do you find yourself having unwanted, vivid memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about the electric shock event?

Yes, I do. Out of nowhere during the day, I’ll suddenly see myself back on that concrete floor staring at my dead arm while the guys are yelling for help, and my chest tightens up like it's happening all over again. I also wake up sweating in the middle of the night from these half-remembered nightmares about work, and I can't get back to sleep after that.
Do you find yourself actively trying to avoid thoughts, feelings, or places—like your workplace—that remind you of the electric shock?

Yes, absolutely. I make up excuses to stay in the office doing paperwork or send the younger apprentices to open panels instead of me. Just the thought of standing in front of live gear makes my stomach flip, and I just can't bring myself to do it.
How long ago did the electric shock accident occur, and how long have you been experiencing these symptoms?
The actual shock happened about six months ago. I tried to shrug it off and joke about it at first, but these symptoms have really been building up and constant for about the last four months.
Since the accident, have you noticed feeling more on edge, easily startled, or constantly on guard, even when you are in a safe environment?

Yes, absolutely. I feel completely wired and jumpy, like I'm constantly on guard and waiting for something terrible to happen. Even when I'm in safe places, like sitting on the couch with my wife or trying to watch a ball game, I just can't shake that feeling.

No other diagnoses are highly indicated, so the candidate remains F43.1.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the diagnostic criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (F43.1). He experienced a life-threatening traumatic event (a severe electric shock at work) 6 months ago. For the past 4 months, he has exhibited characteristic symptoms including intrusive re-experiencing (flashbacks and nightmares), active avoidance of trauma-related stimuli (avoiding electrical gear and delegating hands-on tasks), and persistent hyperarousal (feeling constantly wired, jumpy, and on guard).
